chapters.title: Manufacturing Industries
chapters.summary: In this chapter: manufacturing and its importance; how industries are classified; agro-based industries; mineral-based and other industries.

lessons.title: Manufacturing and its importance

activities.prompt: How do raw materials become the things we use every day?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.prompt: A country grows sugarcane but makes little sugar. How can manufacturing help?
steps: Large-scale sugar production is manufacturing because it processes raw materials into goods.
It belongs to the secondary sector because workers turn primary materials into finished goods.
It can create secondary and tertiary jobs because manufacturing provides employment.
Industrial development can reduce unemployment and poverty, so the country can become stronger.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: A factory turns sugarcane into large amounts of sugar. Why is this manufacturing?
options: It makes goods in large amounts by processing raw materials.
It finds raw sugarcane growing in large fields.
It sells sugarcane without changing the raw material.
It moves sugar to shops without making any goods.

why.It finds raw sugarcane growing in large: Finding a crop does not process raw materials into finished goods.
why.It sells sugarcane without changing the: Selling raw sugarcane does not show large-scale production of goods.
why.It moves sugar to shops without making a: Moving finished goods is not the work of making them.

activities.explanation: It makes goods in large amounts by processing raw materials.

activities.prompt: A town starts manufacturing industries. What is likely in that town?
options: More industrial jobs, with lower unemployment and poverty.
More primary jobs, with lower industrial output.
More factory jobs, with higher unemployment and poverty.
More finished goods, with fewer manufacturing industries.

why.More primary jobs, with lower industrial: It confuses primary-sector work with the secondary manufacturing sector.
why.More factory jobs, with higher unemploym: It wrongly links more factory jobs with higher unemployment and poverty.
why.More finished goods, with fewer manufact: More finished goods do not mean the manufacturing industries will decrease.

activities.explanation: Industrial development can create jobs and help remove unemployment and poverty.

activities.prompt: A map shows sugarcane fields beside a sugar factory. What flow does it suggest?
options: Sugarcane moves into sugar production.
Wood moves into sugar production.
Bauxite moves into sugar production.
Iron ore moves into sugar production.

Wood is used for paper, not for making sugar from sugarcane.
Bauxite is used for aluminium, not for making sugar.
Iron ore is used for iron and steel, not for making sugar.

activities.explanation: Sugar is made from sugarcane, so the map suggests this input flow.

activities.prompt: A country exports more manufactured goods. What benefit can follow?
options: Trade can grow and foreign exchange can enter the country.
Trade can shrink and foreign exchange can leave the country.
Raw materials can enter factories and become finished goods.
Agro-industries can make farm work more productive in the country.

why.Trade can shrink and foreign exchange ca: It reverses both effects of exporting manufactured goods.
why.Raw materials can enter factories and be: It confuses export benefits with the manufacturing process.
why.Agro-industries can make farm work more: It confuses exporting with the effect of agro-industries on farms.

activities.explanation: Exporting manufactured goods can expand trade and bring foreign exchange.

activities.prompt: An agro-industry processes farm sugarcane. How can this help agriculture?
options: It can raise farm productivity and give agriculture a boost.
It can lower farm productivity and reduce farm output.
It can turn primary materials into finished goods only.
It can bring foreign exchange without exporting goods.

why.It can lower farm productivity and reduc: It reverses the effect of agro-industries on farm productivity.
why.It can turn primary materials into finis: It focuses on manufacturing and misses agriculture's major boost.
why.It can bring foreign exchange without ex: It confuses agro-industries with exporting goods for foreign exchange.

activities.explanation: Agro-industries boost agriculture by raising farm productivity.

lessons.title: How industries are classified

activities.prompt: What clues help us sort different industries into groups?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.prompt: Farmers own a cotton-processing business together. They pool resources and share profits or losses by their shares. How should this industry be classified?
steps: Cotton is an agricultural product, so this is agro-based.
The farmers own and operate it, which fits a cooperative.
Pooling resources and proportional sharing confirm the cooperative pattern.
Therefore, it is an agro-based cooperative industry.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: A factory uses cotton as its raw material. Which type does this input show?
options: Agro-based, because cotton is an agricultural product.
Mineral-based, because cotton looks like a mineral.
Consumer industry, because people use the finished cloth.
Basic industry, because cotton helps make other goods.

why.Mineral-based, because cotton looks like: It wrongly treats a farm product as a mineral.
why.Consumer industry, because people use th: It confuses the finished good with the factory's input.
why.Basic industry, because cotton helps mak: Using an input does not mean the factory supplies raw materials.

activities.explanation: Cotton is an agricultural product, so agro-based fits the input.

activities.prompt: One factory supplies raw materials to other factories. Another makes goods people use directly. Which is consumer?
options: The second factory, because people use its goods directly.
The first factory, because other factories use its materials.
Both factories, because both make goods for users.
Neither factory, because direct use must happen at home.

why.The first factory, because other factori: Supplying raw materials makes the first factory a basic industry.
why.Both factories, because both make goods: It mistakes supplying factories for making goods for direct use.
why.Neither factory, because direct use must: It wrongly thinks direct use must happen only at home.

activities.explanation: Consumer industries make goods that people use directly.

activities.prompt: One factory is owned and run by government agencies. Another is owned and run by individuals. Which factory is private?
options: The second factory, because individuals own and run it.
The first factory, because government agencies own and run it.
Both factories, because workers help operate both of them.
Neither factory, because only groups can own industries.

why.The first factory, because government ag: Government ownership and operation describe the first factory instead.
why.Both factories, because workers help ope: It mistakes workers helping with operation for private ownership.
why.Neither factory, because only groups can: It wrongly believes individuals cannot own industries.

activities.explanation: Individuals own and operate private sector industries.

activities.prompt: One factory is run by the state and a group of people. Another is owned and operated by producers. Which factory is joint sector?
options: The first factory, because the state and people run it together.
The second factory, because producers own and operate it.
The first factory, because government agencies can own factories.
Both factories, because each has more than one owner.

why.The second factory, because producers ow: Producers owning and operating it describe a cooperative sector.
why.The first factory, because government ag: It ignores the group's role and focuses on government involvement.
why.Both factories, because each has more th: It wrongly thinks joint sector only means several owners.

activities.explanation: The state and individuals running it together define a joint sector.

activities.prompt: A unit invests one crore rupees in its assets, the stated maximum. Can it meet the small scale rule?
options: Yes, because one crore rupees is the maximum allowed.
No, because small scale units must invest less.
Yes, but only if a government agency owns it.
No, because private units cannot use this limit.

why.No, because small scale units must inves: It wrongly treats the maximum as a limit below one crore.
why.Yes, but only if a government agency own: It wrongly links small scale status to government ownership.
why.No, because private units cannot use thi: It wrongly believes the limit applies only to government units.

activities.explanation: One crore rupees is the present maximum investment allowed.

activities.prompt: One factory makes iron and steel. Another makes light goods from light raw materials. How are they classified?
options: The first is heavy and the second is light.
The first is light and the second is heavy.
Both are heavy because iron and steel are made.
Both are light because both make factory goods.

why.The first is light and the second is hea: It reverses the heavy and light classifications.
why.Both are heavy because iron and steel ar: It ignores that the second factory makes light goods.
why.Both are light because both make factory: It wrongly assumes all factory goods are light.

activities.explanation: Iron and steel are heavy, while light inputs make light industries.

lessons.title: Agro-based industries

activities.prompt: How do textiles, jute, and sugar connect to the industries we see around us?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Agro-based industries
activities.body: Textile production turns raw material into useful, value-added products. The textile industry helps industrial production, employment and foreign exchange earnings. Cotton creates demand for other industries. Weaving is decentralised, so traditional skills and designs can be included. Handspun khadi gives work to home-based weavers. India leads in raw jute and jute goods. India also stands second among sugar producers.
keyPoints: Textiles support production, employment and foreign exchange earnings.
Decentralised weaving includes traditional skills and designs.
India leads in raw jute and jute goods.
activities.explanation: These ideas show production, work, trade and traditional skills.

activities.prompt: A town wants many home weavers. It also wants to keep traditional designs. How should weaving be organised?
steps: Spread weaving among many workers, because weaving is highly decentralised.
Include traditional skills and designs, because decentralised weaving allows this.
Support handspun khadi, because it gives large-scale employment to home weavers.
This can employ many home weavers while keeping traditional skills and designs.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: India's Jute Production
activities.prompt: India is the ______ producer of raw jute and jute goods.
activities.hint: Think about India's place among jute producers.
activities.explanation: India is the largest producer of both raw jute and jute goods.

activities.title: Industry Details
activities.prompt: Match each industry with its correct detail.
pairs: first mill near Kolkata at Rishra
second among the world's sugar producers
activities.explanation: Two pairs describe first mills. The others describe ranking and support for other industries.

activities.title: Benefits of Decentralised Weaving
activities.prompt: Which benefit comes from decentralised weaving?
options: raw jute
sugar output
cotton mills
traditional designs
activities.explanation: Decentralised weaving allows traditional skills and designs to be included.

activities.title: Events in Time Order
activities.prompt: Put these textile and jute events in time order.
items: Power looms came into use after the eighteenth century
First successful textile mill established in Mumbai in 1854
First jute mill set up near Kolkata in 1855 at Rishra
activities.explanation: Power looms came after the eighteenth century. The mills followed in 1854 and 1855.

activities.title: Sugar and Cooperatives
activities.prompt: Why is the sugar industry suitable for the cooperative sector?
options: because it is seasonal
because it exports jute
because it creates demand
because it uses traditional designs
activities.explanation: The sugar industry is seasonal, so it suits the cooperative sector.

activities.title: India's Jute Position
activities.prompt: Which claim about jute production and exports is supported?
options: Bangladesh leads in raw jute production.
India exports more jute than Bangladesh.
India leads in raw jute production.
India leads in jute exports.
activities.explanation: India leads in raw jute production. Bangladesh is ahead in jute exports.

activities.prompt: Which came first, the first textile mill or the first jute mill?
options: The first successful textile mill in Mumbai, in 1854.
The first jute mill near Kolkata at Rishra, in 1855.
The first successful textile mill near Kolkata, in 1854.
The first jute mill in Mumbai, in 1855.

why.The first jute mill near Kolkata at Rish: 1855 is later, so the jute mill did not come first.
why.The first successful textile mill near K: This confuses Mumbai with Rishra, where the jute mill was set up.
This puts the jute mill in Mumbai, but it was near Kolkata.

activities.explanation: 1854 is earlier than 1855, so the textile mill came first.

activities.prompt: A group wants many weavers to work at home. It also wants traditional designs. What should it support?
options: Handspun khadi and decentralised weaving, because both fit the needs.
Handspun khadi and central weaving, because khadi needs one workplace.
Power looms and decentralised weaving, because looms employ home weavers.
Power looms and central weaving, because mills keep traditional designs.

why.Handspun khadi and central weaving, beca: Khadi supports home work, but central weaving weakens the traditional-skills aim.
why.Power looms and decentralised weaving, b: Power looms have no stated connection with employment at home.
why.Power looms and central weaving, because: Central weaving hurts skills, while power looms do not support home work.

activities.explanation: Khadi supports home work, and decentralised weaving includes traditional skills and designs.

activities.prompt: Many sugar workers need one organisation for seasonal work. Which fits?
options: A cooperative, because the sugar industry is seasonal.
A single employer, because seasonal work cannot be shared.
A weaving mill, because sugar production is not seasonal.
Any employer, because seasonal work makes planning unnecessary.

why.A single employer, because seasonal work: This wrongly thinks seasonal work cannot be shared.
why.A weaving mill, because sugar production: This confuses weaving mills with the seasonal sugar industry.
why.Any employer, because seasonal work make: This wrongly treats a seasonal industry as one needing no planning.

activities.explanation: Seasonal sugar work is therefore suitable for the cooperative sector.

activities.prompt: A report compares India and Bangladesh. What should it show about jute?
options: India leads production, but Bangladesh is ahead in jute exports.
India leads exports, because it also leads raw jute production.
Bangladesh leads production, while India exports no jute goods.
Mumbai leads exports, while Rishra leads raw jute production.

why.India leads exports, because it also lea: Largest production does not mean largest exports; India comes second.
why.Bangladesh leads production, while India: India leads production and does export jute goods.
why.Mumbai leads exports, while Rishra leads: The exporter comparison is between India and Bangladesh, not two places.

activities.explanation: India is the largest producer, but it is second only to Bangladesh as an exporter.

lessons.title: Mineral-based and other industries

activities.prompt: Curious about how minerals quietly shape the things we use every day?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Understanding mineral-based industries
activities.body: Mineral-based industries use minerals and metals as raw materials. Iron and steel support other industries through their machinery and products. Chhotanagpur has the greatest concentration of these industries because raw materials and labour are cheap. Aluminium is light, resists corrosion and conducts heat well. Steel production and consumption act as an index, meaning a sign, of a country's development. Bengaluru has emerged as India's electronic capital.
keyPoints: Mineral-based industries use minerals and metals.
Iron and steel support other industries.
Chhotanagpur has the greatest concentration of iron and steel industries.
activities.explanation: These are the main links between minerals, industries and development.

activities.prompt: A steel factory uses minerals and metals as raw materials. Why is Chhotanagpur a strong choice?
steps: The factory is mineral-based because it uses minerals and metals as raw materials.
Chhotanagpur has the greatest concentration of iron and steel industries.
Factories gather there because raw materials and labour are cheap.
So Chhotanagpur is a strong choice for the steel factory.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: What are mineral-based industries?
options: Industries using minerals and metals
Industries making vehicles for transport
Industries producing chemical fertilisers
Industries supplying electricity to homes
activities.explanation: They use minerals and metals as their raw materials.

activities.prompt: Chhotanagpur has the greatest concentration of iron and steel industries because raw materials and labour are cheap.
activities.explanation: Raw materials and labour are cheap in Chhotanagpur.

activities.prompt: Aluminium is light, resists ______ and conducts heat well.
activities.hint: Think of what aluminium can withstand.
activities.explanation: Aluminium resists corrosion and conducts heat well.

activities.prompt: Cement is essential for quick transport of goods and passengers.
activities.explanation: Cement supports construction. Automobiles provide quick transport.

activities.prompt: Match each industry or place with its feature from the lesson.
activities.explanation: Each pair connects an industry or place with its lesson feature.

activities.prompt: A company plans an aluminium smelting unit. Which two requirements must it meet?
options: Regular electricity and assured raw materials
Cheap labour and assured raw materials
Regular electricity and assured vehicles
Regular electricity and assured steel
activities.explanation: Smelting needs regular electricity and an assured raw material source.

activities.prompt: A researcher wants a sign of a country's development. Which measure should they use?
options: Steel production and consumption
Aluminium's light weight
Chemical units' size
Automobiles' passenger capacity
activities.explanation: Steel production and consumption are regarded as an index of development.

activities.prompt: An aluminium factory has power cuts every day. Which need is not properly met?
options: It has no regular electricity supply.
It has no assured source of raw material.
It does not conduct heat well.
It does not resist corrosion.

why.It has no assured source of raw material: The situation shows a power problem, not a raw-material problem.
Power cuts do not change aluminium's ability to conduct heat.
Power cuts do not change aluminium's resistance to corrosion.

activities.explanation: Power cuts prevent the regular electricity that smelting needs.

activities.prompt: Country A produces and uses much more steel than Country B. What does this show?
options: Country A is more developed.
Country B is more developed.
Country A has no other industries.
Country B has more industries.

The comparison shows more steel in Country A, not Country B.
High steel use does not mean there are no other industries.
The facts compare steel use, not the number of industries.

activities.explanation: Steel production and use are regarded as an index of development.

lessons.sceneCaption: Tata Steel plant in Jamshedpur, viewed from Golmuri.

lessons.title: Industrial pollution

activities.prompt: How can industries grow while keeping our air, water, and land healthy?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How industries can pollute
activities.body: Industries help India's economic growth, but they can also seriously pollute the environment. The four main types are air, water, land and noise. Factories, brick kilns, refineries and smelting plants may release smoke. Airborne dust, mist and smoke contain solid or liquid particles. Waste can harm rivers, ponds, soil and living things. Noise can upset people, while nuclear waste can cause serious harm.
keyPoints: Industries support economic growth but can pollute the environment.
The four main types are air, water, land and noise pollution.
Factories can release smoke, dust, mist and liquid particles.
activities.explanation: Learning about industrial pollution helps you understand its effects.

activities.prompt: A factory releases one litre of waste water near a pond. Can it pollute eight litres?
steps: The pond has eight litres, so all fresh water can be affected.
The factory discharges one litre, because industrial waste water can pollute.
One litre can pollute eight litres, because this is the stated ratio.
Therefore, all eight litres of pond water can become polluted.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Harmful effects of pollution
activities.body: Air pollution can harm human health, animals, plants, buildings and the atmosphere. Water pollution comes from organic and inorganic industrial wastes and effluents. Hot factory water can pollute rivers and ponds. Land pollution can make soil useless. Noise pollution can cause irritation, anger, hearing impairment and faster heart rates. Nuclear waste can cause cancers, birth defects and miscarriages.
keyPoints: Air pollution harms people, animals, plants, buildings and the atmosphere.
Industrial wastes, effluents and hot water can pollute water.
Noise and nuclear waste can also cause serious harm.
activities.explanation: Each type of industrial pollution can harm living things and nature.

activities.prompt: Factories, brick kilns, refineries and smelting plants can emit smoke.
activities.explanation: These places can emit smoke. Smoke contributes to air pollution.

activities.prompt: One litre of industrial waste water can pollute ______ litres of fresh water.
activities.hint: Use the number given in the lesson.
activities.explanation: One litre of industrial waste water can pollute eight litres of fresh water.

activities.prompt: Match each source with its effect.
pairs: Factories, brick kilns, refineries and smelting plants
Hot water from factories and thermal plants
Dumped glass, chemicals, effluents, packaging, salts and garbage
activities.explanation: Smoke affects the air. Hot water can harm water bodies. Dumped waste can make soil useless.

activities.prompt: Which group lists effects of noise pollution?
options: irritation, anger, hearing impairment
cancers, birth defects, miscarriages
solid particles, liquid particles
glass, salts, garbage, packaging
activities.explanation: Noise pollution can cause irritation, anger, hearing impairment and faster heart rates.

activities.prompt: Water pollution is caused only by hot water from factories and thermal plants.
activities.explanation: Hot water can pollute rivers and ponds. Organic and inorganic industrial wastes and effluents also cause water pollution.

activities.prompt: Waste from nuclear plants and weapons facilities can cause cancers, ______ and miscarriages.
activities.hint: Think of the effects listed in the lesson.
activities.explanation: Waste from nuclear plants and weapons facilities can cause cancers, birth defects and miscarriages.

activities.prompt: A brick kiln makes smoke. A factory releases hot water into a pond. How do their effects differ?
options: Smoke can harm health; hot water can pollute the pond.
Smoke can pollute the pond; hot water can harm hearing.
Smoke can make soil useless; hot water can clean the river.
Smoke can raise heart rates; hot water can improve buildings.

why.Smoke can pollute the pond; hot water ca: This wrongly assigns water and noise effects to the wrong sources.
why.Smoke can make soil useless; hot water c: This wrongly confuses smoke with land waste and pollution with cleaning.
why.Smoke can raise heart rates; hot water c: This wrongly links smoke with noise effects and treats hot water as helpful.

activities.explanation: Smoke can harm health, and hot water can pollute ponds.

activities.prompt: A map shows a refinery beside a town. What can the map suggest about smoke risks?
options: The town may face smoke-related health harms.
The map proves every town person is already ill.
The refinery cannot affect the town because it is outside.
The map proves no factory smoke can leave the site.

why.The map proves every town person is alre: This wrongly treats map proximity as proof that everyone is ill.
why.The refinery cannot affect the town beca: This wrongly assumes pollution cannot travel beyond the factory site.
why.The map proves no factory smoke can leav: This wrongly assumes a map proves that smoke stays at one place.

activities.explanation: Refineries can emit smoke, and smoke can harm people's health.

activities.prompt: A local rule limits a factory to one litre of waste water. How much fresh water can it pollute?
options: Eight litres of fresh water.
One litre of fresh water.
Four litres of fresh water.
Eighty litres of fresh water.

This wrongly uses the same amount instead of the stated ratio.
This wrongly halves the stated amount instead of following the rule.
This wrongly multiplies the amount instead of using eight litres.

activities.explanation: This is right: one litre can pollute eight litres of fresh water.

activities.prompt: A nuclear plant stores waste near homes. Factories dump glass and chemicals on land. How do the risks differ?
options: Nuclear waste can cause cancers; dumped waste can make soil useless.
Nuclear waste can make soil useless; dumped glass can cause miscarriages.
Nuclear waste can cause hearing loss; dumped waste can reduce factory smoke.
Nuclear waste can improve buildings; dumped waste can cool nearby rivers.

why.Nuclear waste can make soil useless; dum: This wrongly swaps the effects of nuclear waste and dumped factory waste.
why.Nuclear waste can cause hearing loss; du: This wrongly treats nuclear waste as a noise source and pollution as helpful.
why.Nuclear waste can improve buildings; dum: This wrongly treats nuclear waste as helpful and ignores land damage.

activities.explanation: Nuclear waste can cause cancers, and dumped waste can make soil useless.

lessons.title: Controlling environmental degradation

activities.prompt: How can we help industries grow while caring for water, air, and people?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Controlling industrial harm
activities.body: Industries can protect water by reusing it through several stages and collecting rainwater. Hot water and effluents need treatment before entering rivers and ponds. Effluents move through primary, secondary and tertiary treatment. Smoke stacks can use filters and scrubbers. Generators can use silencers. People can use earplugs, earphones and noise-absorbing materials. Sustainable development joins economic development with environmental concerns.
keyPoints: Reuse water and collect rainwater.
Treat hot water and effluents before release.
Use filters, scrubbers and silencers.
activities.explanation: Industries can reduce environmental harm through careful water, waste and noise control.

activities.prompt: A factory uses too much groundwater and releases hot water into a pond. What should it change?
steps: First, it should treat hot water and effluents before release, because rivers and ponds should receive treated water.
Next, it should reuse and recycle water through successive stages, because industries can reuse water in several stages.
It should collect rainwater, because rainwater can meet its industrial water requirements.
Finally, it should regulate groundwater overdrawing legally, because sustainable development joins industry’s needs with environmental care.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Careful development
activities.body: Primary treatment uses mechanical methods such as screening, grinding, flocculation and sedimentation. Groundwater overdrawing needs legal rules. Green belts can support ecological balance around power stations. NTPC has ISO certification for its Environment Management System. Sustainable development needs economic development and environmental concerns to work together.
keyPoints: Primary treatment uses mechanical methods.
Legal rules can control groundwater overdrawing.
Green belts can support ecological balance.
activities.explanation: Development should protect groundwater, nature and the environment.

activities.prompt: Why should generators have silencers fitted?
options: To increase noise
To treat water
To reduce noise
To collect rainwater
activities.explanation: Silencers reduce noise from generators.

activities.prompt: Match each problem with a suitable control method.
activities.explanation: Each method helps control a different form of environmental harm.

activities.prompt: Which action belongs to primary treatment?
options: Fitting a silencer
Collecting rainwater
Screening and sedimentation
Using earplugs
activities.explanation: Primary treatment uses mechanical methods, including screening and sedimentation.

activities.prompt: Put the industrial effluent treatment stages in order.
activities.explanation: The stages run from primary to secondary and then tertiary.

activities.prompt: What must work with environmental concerns?
options: Rainwater collection
Economic development
Noise reduction
Water reuse
activities.explanation: Sustainable development integrates economic development with environmental concerns.

activities.prompt: NTPC has ______ certification for its Environment Management System.
activities.hint: This certification manages environmental work at NTPC.
activities.explanation: NTPC has ISO certification for its Environment Management System.

activities.prompt: A factory is overdrawing groundwater. Which water plan is sensible?
options: Reuse water, collect rainwater, and regulate groundwater overdrawing legally.
Reuse nothing, collect no rain, and pump groundwater freely.
Treat only smoke, and ignore all water reuse and collection.
Release untreated effluents, and avoid collecting any rainwater.

why.Reuse nothing, collect no rain, and pump: This ignores water reuse, rainwater collection and legal regulation.
why.Treat only smoke, and ignore all water r: This confuses smoke control with managing industrial water.
why.Release untreated effluents, and avoid c: This confuses releasing waste with managing water.

activities.explanation: This combines water reuse, rainwater collection and legal groundwater control.

activities.prompt: A factory has dirty effluent and smoke stacks. Which plan treats both problems correctly?
options: Use mechanical effluent treatment; fit filters and scrubbers on smoke stacks.
Use generator silencers for effluent; fit filters on smoke stacks.
Use earplugs for effluent; fit filters on smoke stacks.
Use rain collection for effluent; fit filters on smoke stacks.

why.Use generator silencers for effluent; fi: Silencers reduce noise, not dirty effluent.
why.Use earplugs for effluent; fit filters o: Earplugs protect hearing, but they do not treat effluent.
why.Use rain collection for effluent; fit fi: Rainwater collection supplies water, but it does not treat effluent.

activities.explanation: Mechanical methods treat effluent, while filters and scrubbers reduce airborne particles.

activities.prompt: Homes are near noisy factory generators. Which plan reduces noise and protects workers?
options: Fit generator silencers and give workers earplugs.
Fit generator filters and give workers earplugs.
Fit generator scrubbers and give workers earphones.
Fit smoke-stack filters and place green belts nearby.

why.Fit generator filters and give workers e: Filters reduce airborne particles, but they do not reduce generator noise.
why.Fit generator scrubbers and give workers: Scrubbers reduce airborne particles, but they do not reduce generator noise.
why.Fit smoke-stack filters and place green: Smoke-stack filters and green belts do not reduce generator noise.

activities.explanation: Silencers reduce generator noise, and earplugs protect workers’ hearing.

activities.prompt: An NTPC power station grows and has ISO Environment Management certification. It also wants green belts. What does this show?
options: Economic development is being joined with environmental care.
Only economic development matters, so environmental steps do not count.
Only environmental care matters, so economic development should stop.
Economic and environmental actions must always happen separately.

why.Only economic development matters, so en: This believes economic development must ignore environmental concerns.
why.Only environmental care matters, so econ: This believes economic growth and environmental care must oppose each other.
why.Economic and environmental actions must: This believes development and environmental care cannot be joined.

activities.explanation: Certification and green belts join development with environmental care.

activities.context: A paper mill processes wood into large quantities of paper, while workers in the secondary sector operate its machinery. A nearby sugar mill turns sugarcane into sugar, and its agro-industry links help farmers raise productivity. The manufacturers sell goods overseas, expanding trade and earning foreign exchange. To keep selling in international markets, the mills must make sure their goods match the quality expected there.
activities.prompt: If the mills fail to match the quality of goods in the international market, what is most likely to happen next?
options: Their goods may be rejected in international markets, reducing exports and foreign exchange.
Their goods will gain more trade and bring more foreign exchange because they are locally made.
Their goods will sell more widely overseas, so the country's trade and foreign exchange will increase.
Only domestic buyers will be affected, while export trade and foreign exchange will remain unchanged.

why.Their goods will gain more trade and bri: Local production alone does not guarantee acceptance in international markets.
why.Their goods will sell more widely overse: Foreign exchange cannot be expected to increase if exports are rejected.
why.Only domestic buyers will be affected, w: A fall in exports can also affect trade and foreign exchange.

activities.explanation: Goods that do not match international quality may be rejected.

activities.context: A paper mill processes wood into large quantities of paper, while workers in the secondary sector operate its machinery. A nearby sugar mill turns sugarcane into sugar, and its agro-industry links help farmers raise productivity. The manufacturers sell goods overseas, expanding trade and earning foreign exchange. To keep selling in international markets, the mills must make sure their goods match the quality expected there.
activities.prompt: Which policy best supports industrial development as a way to reduce unemployment and poverty?
options: Develop manufacturing industries so they can provide jobs in the secondary and tertiary sectors.
Expand only primary-material collection and leave manufacturing industries underdeveloped.
Build manufacturing industries but refuse to create jobs outside manufacturing itself.
Raise manufactured exports without checking whether the goods match international-market quality.

why.Expand only primary-material collection: Expanding primary-material collection does not develop manufacturing industries.
why.Build manufacturing industries but refus: Manufacturing industries can provide jobs in both secondary and tertiary sectors.
why.Raise manufactured exports without check: Indian manufactured goods must match international-market quality.

activities.explanation: Industrial development helps remove unemployment and poverty.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Manufacturing industries are part of the secondary sector.
Reason (R): Workers in the secondary sector turn primary materials into finished goods.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The reason explains the classification because manufacturing turns primary materials into finished goods.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Manufacturing industries are part of the primary sector.
Reason (R): Manufacturing industries are part of the secondary sector.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is false because manufacturing industries belong to the secondary sector.

activities.prompt: What is the difference between manufacturing and primary-material work?
activities.answer: Manufacturing means producing goods in large quantities by processing raw materials. Primary-material work supplies the inputs, such as wood, sugarcane, iron ore, or bauxite. Workers in the secondary sector turn those primary materials into finished goods, so manufacturing industries belong to the secondary sector. For example, wood becomes paper and sugarcane becomes sugar. Thus, the main difference is that manufacturing changes primary materials into finished goods, rather than merely providing the primary materials used in production.
points: Manufacturing processes raw materials into goods in large quantities.
Primary-material work provides inputs such as wood, sugarcane, iron ore and bauxite.
Secondary-sector workers turn primary materials into finished goods.
Paper comes from wood, while sugar is made from sugarcane.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A cooperative of tea growers in a farming area processes tea and sells the finished product. A government agency runs an iron and steel plant in the same region. A private business makes consumer goods, while another producer group shares resources and profits or losses proportionately. One business plans to replace its machinery and will invest more than one crore rupees in its unit’s assets.
activities.prompt: If the last business carries out its plan, what can be concluded about its classification?
options: It cannot be classified as a small scale industry.
It must remain a small scale industry because it was already operating.
It will become a joint sector industry because its investment is increasing.
It will become a basic industry because it is using machinery.

why.It must remain a small scale industry be: A planned increase in investment does not preserve the earlier limit.
why.It will become a joint sector industry b: A larger investment does not change ownership into a state-private partnership.
why.It will become a basic industry because: The use of machinery does not make an industry a supplier of raw materials.

activities.explanation: Small scale status depends on the permitted maximum investment.

activities.context: A cooperative of tea growers in a farming area processes tea and sells the finished product. A government agency runs an iron and steel plant in the same region. A private business makes consumer goods, while another producer group shares resources and profits or losses proportionately. One business plans to replace its machinery and will invest more than one crore rupees in its unit’s assets.
activities.prompt: If one member of the cooperative contributes more resources than the others and the business earns a profit, what should that member receive?
options: A larger proportion of the profit, with losses also shared proportionately.
Exactly the same amount as every member, regardless of the contribution.
No part of the profit, because only the producers can share the results.
A smaller proportion of the profit because larger contributions reduce the profit.

why.Exactly the same amount as every member,: Proportionate sharing does not require equal amounts from all members.
why.No part of the profit, because only the: Contributing resources makes the member part of the sharing arrangement.
why.A smaller proportion of the profit becau: A larger contribution should lead to a proportionately larger share.

activities.explanation: Cooperatives distribute profits and losses in proportion to pooled resources.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The tea-processing unit is agro-based because it uses tea.
Reason (R): Tea is an agricultural product used by agro-based industries.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Both statements are true, and the agricultural nature of tea explains the classification.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The government agency’s iron and steel plant is a public sector industry.
Reason (R): The plant is jointly run by the state and individuals or groups.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The plant is public sector, but it is run by a government agency rather than jointly by the state and individuals or groups.

activities.prompt: Explain how the businesses in the case can be classified in more than one way.
activities.answer: The tea business is agro-based because it processes tea, an agricultural product. It is cooperative sector because producers operate it and pool their resources. If its investment in a unit’s assets does not exceed one crore rupees, it is also a small scale industry. The iron and steel plant is mineral-based because iron and steel are included in that category. It is heavy because iron and steel are included among heavy industries, and it is public sector because a government agency owns and operates it. These classifications describe different features of a business.
points: Identifies the tea business as agro-based.
Explains the cooperative classification of the tea business.
Links small scale status to the one-crore-rupee investment limit.
Classifies the iron and steel plant by product, type and ownership.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: A weaving family earns income by spinning khadi and working at home. A nearby textile mill uses power looms and produces value-added textile goods. In another region, sugar production changes with the season, so producers are considering a cooperative. An exporter is also planning how to respond if Indian jute goods become more popular abroad, since India is the largest producer of raw jute and jute goods but is second only to Bangladesh as an exporter.
activities.prompt: If the weaving family moved from home-based khadi work to centralised power-loom weaving, which effect would be most likely?
options: They would lose large-scale home employment and the chance to include traditional designs.
They would gain large-scale home employment but lose the chance to include traditional designs.
They would gain the chance to include traditional designs but lose large-scale home employment.
They would gain both large-scale home employment and the chance to include traditional designs.

why.They would gain large-scale home employm: Decentralised weaving allows traditional skills and designs to be included.
why.They would gain the chance to include tr: Home-based khadi work makes such employment possible.
why.They would gain both large-scale home em: Centralised power-loom weaving does not provide either of these features.

activities.explanation: Handspun khadi supports large-scale home-based employment.

activities.context: A weaving family earns income by spinning khadi and working at home. A nearby textile mill uses power looms and produces value-added textile goods. In another region, sugar production changes with the season, so producers are considering a cooperative. An exporter is also planning how to respond if Indian jute goods become more popular abroad, since India is the largest producer of raw jute and jute goods but is second only to Bangladesh as an exporter.
activities.prompt: If cotton production rises and the cotton industry continues to create demand for other industries, what should be expected?
options: Demand in the other industries will rise.
Demand in the other industries will fall.
Other industries will stop creating their own demand.
Demand in the other industries will remain unchanged.

why.Demand in the other industries will fall: Increased production would not be expected to reduce that demand.
why.Other industries will stop creating thei: Other industries also create demand through their activities.
why.Demand in the other industries will rema: The effect of greater cotton production is increased, not unchanged, demand.

activities.explanation: The cotton industry supports other industries by creating demand.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): The cooperative sector is suitable for the sugar industry.
Reason (R): The sugar industry is seasonal.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: Seasonal production is the reason the cooperative sector is suitable for the sugar industry.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): India is second only to Bangladesh as an exporter of jute goods.
Reason (R): India is the smallest producer of raw jute and jute goods.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The assertion is true, but the reason is false because India is the largest producer.

activities.prompt: How does the self-reliant nature of the textile industry differ from the decentralised nature of weaving?
activities.answer: The textile industry is self-reliant because it covers the complete journey from raw material to highly value-added products. This complete structure helps it contribute greatly to industrial production, employment and foreign exchange earnings. Weaving, however, is highly decentralised. This allows traditional skills and designs to be included. Handspun khadi provides large-scale employment to weavers working in their homes. Thus, self-reliance describes the range of activities in the textile industry, while decentralisation describes the dispersed organisation of weaving and the inclusion of traditional work.
points: Textile production covers raw material to value-added products.
The textile industry supports production, employment and foreign exchange earnings.
Weaving is highly decentralised.
Traditional skills, designs and home-based khadi employment are possible.
activities.explanation: Compare your answer with the points a marker looks for.

activities.context: Ravi’s family wants to start an electronics manufacturing unit in Bengaluru, where vehicles can carry goods to different markets. The unit will need regular electricity and a dependable supply of raw material for aluminium parts, while builders require cement for houses and bridges. Ravi is also considering an iron and steel unit in Chhotanagpur, but estimates that cheap raw materials and labour are needed to compete in the highly concentrated industry.
activities.prompt: If the regular electricity supply for aluminium smelting becomes unreliable, what is the most likely result?
options: The smelting process would lose its regular power and could not continue reliably.
Aluminium parts would become heavier and conduct heat poorly.
The parts would become more resistant to corrosion.
The aluminium would conduct heat better because electricity had fallen.

why.Aluminium parts would become heavier and: Nothing given would make aluminium heavier.
why.The aluminium would conduct heat better: Less power would not improve heat conduction.

activities.explanation: Aluminium smelting requires a regular electricity supply.

activities.context: Ravi’s family wants to start an electronics manufacturing unit in Bengaluru, where vehicles can carry goods to different markets. The unit will need regular electricity and a dependable supply of raw material for aluminium parts, while builders require cement for houses and bridges. Ravi is also considering an iron and steel unit in Chhotanagpur, but estimates that cheap raw materials and labour are needed to compete in the highly concentrated industry.
activities.prompt: Why is Bengaluru a suitable location for Ravi’s electronics manufacturing unit?
options: Bengaluru has become India’s center for a broad range of electronic products.
Chhotanagpur has become India’s center for a broad range of electronic products.
Bengaluru has become India’s center for iron and steel production.
Bengaluru has become India’s center for cement production.

why.Chhotanagpur has become India’s center f: The electronic capital is Bengaluru, not Chhotanagpur.
why.Bengaluru has become India’s center for: Chhotanagpur is associated with iron and steel industries.
Cement is essential for construction but is not located specifically in Bengaluru.

activities.explanation: Bengaluru has emerged as India’s electronic capital.

activities.prompt:
Assertion (A): Iron and steel form the basic industry.
Reason (R): Other industries depend on their machinery and products.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
activities.explanation: The dependence of other industries explains why iron and steel form the basic industry.

boss.title: Chapter challenge: Manufacturing Industries

activities.prompt: What does manufacturing mean?
options: Producing goods in small amounts by hand
Producing goods in large quantities by processing raw materials
Selling goods without making them
Using finished goods to make services
activities.explanation: Manufacturing means producing goods in large quantities by processing raw materials.

activities.prompt: Agro-based industries use agricultural products such as cotton, jute, sugar and tea.
activities.explanation: Yes. These industries use agricultural products to make goods.

activities.prompt: Match each manufactured product with its raw material.
activities.explanation: Great matching. Each product is made by processing the raw material beside it.

activities.prompt: Manufacturing industries belong to the ______ sector.
activities.hint: Workers turn primary materials into finished goods.
activities.explanation: Correct. Manufacturing industries are part of the secondary sector.

activities.prompt: Which activity expands trade and brings foreign exchange into a country?
options: Exporting manufactured goods
Importing raw materials only
Stopping all industrial production
Keeping goods inside the country
activities.explanation: Exporting manufactured goods expands trade and brings foreign exchange into the country.

activities.prompt: Match each sector with its owners or operators.
pairs: the state and individuals or groups
activities.explanation: Excellent. Each sector has a different group owning or operating it.

activities.prompt: Put the stages of industrial effluent treatment in order.
activities.explanation: Well done. Industrial effluents are treated in primary, secondary and tertiary stages.

activities.prompt: Which city has emerged as the electronic capital of India?
options: Kolkata
Bengaluru
Mumbai
Rishra
activities.explanation: Bengaluru has emerged as the electronic capital of India.

activities.prompt: Hot water from factories and thermal plants cannot pollute rivers and ponds.
activities.explanation: It can pollute rivers and ponds. Treating hot water before release helps protect water.

activities.prompt: What does sustainable development require?
options: Economic growth without environmental care
Environmental care without economic development
Economic development integrated with environmental concerns
Only more factories and no pollution checks
activities.explanation: Correct. Sustainable development combines economic development with environmental concerns.

chapters.title: Lifelines of National Economy
chapters.summary: In this chapter: transport and roadways; railways and pipelines; waterways and sea ports; airways.

lessons.title: Transport and Roadways

activities.prompt: How does transport connect people, goods, and services across different places?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Why Transport Matters
activities.body: Transport moves goods and services from where they are produced to where people need them. Efficient transport helps a country develop faster. There are three main types: land, water and air. Roads cost much less to build than railway lines. They give door-to-door service, so goods can be collected and delivered directly. This reduces loading and unloading costs. Roads also link railway stations, airports and seaports.
keyPoints: Transport moves goods and services to where they are needed.
Land, water and air are the main transport types.
Roads give door-to-door service and support other transport systems.
activities.explanation: Transport connects production with people, while roads offer useful and affordable links.

activities.prompt: How can goods move from a station to a nearby shop?
steps: Goods cannot reach the shop without transport because they are produced elsewhere.
Road transport is suitable because it gives door-to-door service.
This service reduces loading and unloading costs for the shop.
Therefore, a road can move the goods directly to the shop.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: What Transport Moves
activities.prompt: What does transport help move?
options: Goods and services
People and offices
Farms and forests
Shops and hospitals
activities.explanation: Transport carries goods and services from where they are produced to where they are needed.

activities.title: Roads and Their Work
activities.prompt: Match each road name with its work.
pairs: Connect a state capital with district headquarters
Builds and maintains roads in border areas
Links every village with a major town
Link railway stations, airports and seaports
activities.explanation: Each organisation or road type has a clear role in India’s road network.

activities.title: A Village's Motorable Link
activities.prompt: Every village should link to a major town by a ______ road.
activities.hint: This scheme wants every village to reach a major town.
activities.explanation: The rural road scheme aims to provide this motorable link.

activities.title: Door-to-Door Service
activities.prompt: Why does road transport reduce loading and unloading costs?
options: Because it gives door-to-door service
Because it uses many loading points
Because it needs extra road repairs
Because it carries goods by air
activities.explanation: Door-to-door service collects and delivers goods directly. This reduces loading and unloading costs.

activities.title: Roads Support Other Transport
activities.prompt: Which work do roads do for other transport systems?
options: Link stations, airports and seaports
Carry ships on inland rivers
Provide all passenger flights
Replace the railway system
activities.explanation: Roads feed other transport systems by linking their stations, airports and seaports.

activities.title: Choosing the Right Scheme
activities.prompt: Which scheme links every village to a major town by a motorable road?
options: The rural road scheme
The Super Highways project
State Highways
The Border Roads Organisation
activities.explanation: The rural road scheme aims to give every village a motorable link with a major town.

activities.prompt: A shop gets goods from a railway station. Why can a road help?
options: Roads give door-to-door service but increase loading costs.
It gives door-to-door service and reduces loading costs.
Roads need many reloads because they end at stations.
The road connects a capital with a district headquarters.

why.Roads give door-to-door service but incr: This mistake reverses the effect of door-to-door service on loading costs.
why.Roads need many reloads because they end: This mistake assumes roads do not link railway stations.
why.The road connects a capital with a distr: This mistake treats the delivery road as a State Highway.

activities.explanation: Door-to-door service reduces loading and unloading costs for the shop.

activities.prompt: A road joins a railway station, an airport, and a seaport. What does it do?
options: It replaces all three connected transport systems.
It links three transport systems in one place.
It works only for goods, not services.
It closes the other transport systems nearby.

why.It replaces all three connected transpor: This mistake thinks a linking road replaces the systems it joins.
This mistake separates goods from services in transport.
why.It closes the other transport systems ne: This mistake thinks linking a place means closing it.

activities.explanation: Roads feed other systems by linking stations, airports, and seaports.

activities.prompt: A government wants faster development but has little money. Why choose roads?
options: Building roads costs more, but efficient transport still helps.
Building roads costs less, but efficient transport cannot help.
Building roads costs less, so development stops without railways.
Building roads costs less, and efficient transport helps development.

why.Building roads costs more, but efficient: This mistake reverses the lower cost of building roads.
why.Building roads costs less, but efficient: This mistake denies that efficient transport helps a country develop faster.
why.Building roads costs less, so developmen: This mistake assumes development must always use railway lines.

activities.explanation: Building roads costs less, and efficient transport helps countries develop faster.

lessons.title: Railways and Pipelines

activities.prompt: How do trains and pipelines move so many things across India?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: How Railways and Pipelines Work
activities.body: Railways carry freight and passengers across India. Freight means goods, while passengers are people who travel. The first train travelled from Mumbai to Thane in 1853. Indian Railways has 17 zones, or main groups. Flat northern plains suit railway lines. Hilly routes use low hills, gaps and tunnels. Pipelines cost much to lay, but little to run. They carry crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas.
keyPoints: Railways carry freight and passengers across India.
Indian Railways has 17 zones.
Pipelines carry crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas.
activities.explanation: This lesson shows how railways and pipelines move goods and people.

activities.prompt: A company must move petroleum products. It wants cheap running costs after setup. Should it use a pipeline?
steps: A pipeline fits because it can carry petroleum products.
Pipelines avoid trans-shipment losses and delays because cargo is not lost.
However, laying a pipeline costs a lot at first.
Choose a pipeline when later running costs matter more than setup costs.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which pair do Indian railways mainly carry?
options: food and clothing
freight and passengers
letters and newspapers
machines and medicine
activities.explanation: Railways are India's main way of carrying freight and passengers. Good work!

activities.prompt: Indian Railways is divided into ______ zones.
activities.hint: Think of the number of railway zones.
activities.explanation: Indian Railways is divided into 17 zones. That was the missing number!

activities.prompt: Put the pipeline stages in order.
items: Lay the pipeline at a high cost
Run the pipeline at a low cost
activities.explanation: Laying comes first and costs a lot. Running later costs little, and cargo does not get lost during transfer.

activities.prompt: Match each place or transport with its lesson fact.
pairs: use low hills, gaps and tunnels
activities.explanation: Each pair matches the place, route or transport with the fact given in your book.

activities.prompt: Why do pipelines avoid transfer losses and delays?
options: They stop at many different loading points.
They use many other transport vehicles.
They do not lose cargo during transfer.
They need regular unloading at each stop.
activities.explanation: Pipelines do not lose cargo during transfer. This avoids transfer losses and delays.

activities.prompt: A firm wants to move crude oil without losing cargo during transfer. Which transport should it use?
options: A pipeline, because it avoids cargo loss in transfer.
A railway, because hilly routes always use tunnels.
A pipeline, because it is cheap to lay at first.
A railway, because Konkan railway serves every area.
activities.explanation: Pipelines carry crude oil and avoid cargo loss during transfer. That meets the firm's need.

activities.prompt: A map shows India's west coast. Which project would improve movement there?
options: Build the Konkan railway along the coast.
Build railway lines across northern plains.
Build more railway zones along the coast.
Carry crude oil through coastal pipelines.

why.Build railway lines across northern plai: The northern plains fact concerns good conditions for building railway lines.
why.Build more railway zones along the coast: More zones do not mean more railway lines or better movement.
why.Carry crude oil through coastal pipeline: The fact about better coast movement names the Konkan railway.

activities.explanation: The Konkan railway improved passenger and goods movement along India's west coast.

activities.prompt: A map shows plains and hills. Which route needs tunnels more often?
options: The route through hilly land.
The route through flat plains.
The route inside a railway zone.
The route carrying natural gas.

Flat northern plains give good conditions for building railway lines.
Zones organise railways, not the land shape of a route.
Natural gas moves through pipelines, not as a railway route.

activities.explanation: Hilly railway lines pass through low hills, gaps and tunnels.

activities.prompt: A firm can pay setup costs now. It wants lower running costs later. Which fits?
options: Use a pipeline for petroleum products.
Build railway lines through hilly tunnels.
Avoid railway property damage with ticketless travel.
Organise railways into seventeen zones.

why.Build railway lines through hilly tunnel: Tunnels change hilly railway routes; they do not ensure low running costs.
why.Avoid railway property damage with ticke: Ticketless travel is a railway problem, not a low-cost choice.
Zones divide Indian Railways; they do not control transport running costs.

activities.explanation: Pipelines have high setup costs, but low running costs later.

activities.prompt: A company wants to move crude oil. It wants no cargo loss during transfer. What should it use?
options: Use a pipeline carrying crude oil.
Use a railway through hilly tunnels.
Use a passenger train across plains.
Use one line inside a railway zone.

Hilly tunnels guide railway lines; they do not prevent cargo loss.
Passenger trains carry people; this fact gives no cargo protection.
Zones organise railways, while pipelines move oil without transfer loss.

activities.explanation: Pipelines carry crude oil and avoid cargo loss during transfer.

activities.prompt: A family must travel and send goods. Which choice uses India's main transport system?
options: Use railways for freight and passengers.
Use pipelines for freight and passengers.
Use railway zones for freight and passengers.
Use railway tunnels for freight and passengers.

why.Use pipelines for freight and passengers: Pipelines carry crude oil, petroleum products and natural gas, not passengers.
why.Use railway zones for freight and passen: Zones organise railways; they are not a transport service.
why.Use railway tunnels for freight and pass: Tunnels are railway route parts, not a separate transport service.

activities.explanation: Railways are India's main way of carrying freight and passengers.

lessons.title: Waterways and Sea Ports

activities.prompt: How do waterways help India move goods, and why do some ports stand out?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Moving Goods Through Water
activities.body: Waterways are the cheapest way to transport goods. They suit heavy and bulky items well. India has 14,500 km of inland navigation waterways. About 95 per cent of India’s trade volume moves by sea. Mumbai is India’s biggest port and has a spacious natural harbour. Mormugao in Goa mainly exports iron ore. Chennai is an old artificial port. Vishakhapatnam is the deepest, landlocked and well-protected port.
keyPoints: Waterways are cheapest for transport.
They suit heavy and bulky goods.
Sea carries about 95 per cent of trade.
activities.explanation: This lesson connects cheap transport, heavy goods, and India’s ports.

activities.prompt: A business wants to move heavy, bulky goods to another place. Should it use a waterway?
steps: Waterways are the cheapest form of transport, so they help a business save money.
They are also especially suitable for heavy and bulky goods, so they fit this shipment.
Therefore, the business should use a waterway for these goods.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.prompt: Which form of transport is the cheapest?
options: Waterway transport
Air transport
Road transport
Rail transport
activities.explanation: Waterways are the cheapest form of transport.

activities.prompt: India has ______ km of inland navigation waterways.
activities.hint: Choose the inland navigation distance from your book.
activities.explanation: India has 14,500 km of inland navigation waterways.

activities.prompt: Waterways suit carrying heavy and bulky goods.
activities.explanation: Yes, waterways are especially suitable for heavy and bulky goods.

activities.prompt: Which port is India’s main iron ore exporting port?
options: Chennai
Vishakhapatnam
Mormugao
Mumbai
activities.explanation: Mormugao port in Goa is the country’s main iron ore exporting port.

activities.prompt: Match each port description with the correct port.
pairs: One of India’s oldest artificial ports
activities.explanation: Each description shows a special feature of its port.

activities.prompt: Which port and description are correctly paired?
options: Mumbai — spacious natural harbour
Mormugao — oldest artificial port
Chennai — main iron ore exporter
Vishakhapatnam — biggest Indian port
activities.explanation: Mumbai is India’s biggest port and has a spacious natural harbour.

activities.prompt: Waterways suit heavy, bulky goods. Which should a factory use to send them?
options: Use a waterway because it is cheap and suits heavy goods.
Use a road because it always costs less for every load.
Use air because heavy and bulky goods always travel faster.
Use a railway because water cannot carry heavy goods at all.

why.Use a road because it always costs less: This wrongly treats roads as always cheaper than waterways.
why.Use air because heavy and bulky goods al: This wrongly assumes heavy goods always travel faster by air.
why.Use a railway because water cannot carry: This wrongly believes waterways cannot carry heavy goods.

activities.explanation: Waterways cost less and suit heavy, bulky goods.

activities.prompt: India has 14,500 km of inland waterways. What does this show?
options: India has an extensive system for inland water travel.
Every Indian city must have a navigable waterway.
All of India's goods move through these waterways.
India has no need for sea ports or other transport.

why.Every Indian city must have a navigable: This wrongly assumes every city has a navigable waterway.
why.All of India's goods move through these: This wrongly claims that all goods use inland waterways.
why.India has no need for sea ports or other: This wrongly believes sea ports and other transport are unnecessary.

activities.explanation: The 14,500 km length shows an extensive inland waterway system.

activities.prompt: Waterways suit heavy, bulky goods. A map shows one route. Why is it useful?
options: It offers cheap transport for heavy and bulky goods.
It guarantees every load will reach its destination on time.
It proves sea transport is unimportant to India's trade.
It is suitable only for light and small goods.

why.It guarantees every load will reach its: This wrongly assumes waterways guarantee delivery on time.
why.It proves sea transport is unimportant t: This wrongly treats one waterway as proof against sea trade.
why.It is suitable only for light and small: This wrongly claims waterways suit only light, small goods.

activities.explanation: The route offers cheap transport that suits heavy, bulky goods.

activities.prompt: About 95 per cent of India's trade moves by sea. Why might a port need more loading space?
options: Because most of India's trade reaches ports by sea.
Because most Indian trade moves inland by road.
Because only a small part of trade uses sea routes.
Because all Indian trade already travels by air.

why.Because most Indian trade moves inland b: This wrongly replaces the main sea trade route with roads.
why.Because only a small part of trade uses: This wrongly claims that sea routes carry only a small part.
why.Because all Indian trade already travels: This wrongly claims that all trade already moves by air.

activities.explanation: Most trade moves by sea, so ports need room to load it.

activities.prompt: Mormugao is Goa's main iron ore exporting port. Which port should an exporter use, and why?
options: Mormugao, because it mainly exports iron ore.
Mumbai, because its size suits every cargo.
Chennai, because its age makes it best for iron ore.
Vishakhapatnam, because depth makes it the main iron port.

why.Mumbai, because its size suits every car: This confuses being India's biggest port with exporting iron ore.
why.Chennai, because its age makes it best f: This confuses being an old artificial port with exporting iron ore.
why.Vishakhapatnam, because depth makes it t: This confuses being the deepest landlocked port with exporting iron ore.

activities.explanation: This matches Mormugao's role as India's main iron ore exporting port.

lessons.title: Airways

activities.prompt: How do planes and helicopters connect places people find hard to reach?
activities.explanation: Now read on to find out.

activities.title: Airways at Work
activities.body: Air travel is the fastest, most comfortable and most prestigious transport. Prestigious means known and respected. It makes difficult and remote areas easier to reach. The Regional Connectivity Scheme is called UDAN. It was designed to start the regional aviation market. UDAN aims to make flying affordable for ordinary citizens. Helicopter services support oil and natural gas operations in inaccessible areas.
keyPoints: Air travel is fast, comfortable and respected.
UDAN starts the regional aviation market and supports affordable flying.
Helicopters support oil and natural gas operations in inaccessible areas.
activities.explanation: These are the main ideas about air travel and helicopters.

activities.prompt: Floods and forests make land travel difficult in a northern area. Could flying help ordinary people there?
steps: Floods and forests make land travel difficult in northern and eastern areas.
Air travel helps because it makes remote areas easier to reach.
UDAN supports regional routes through useful policies and incentives.
UDAN aims to make this flying affordable for ordinary citizens.
activities.explanation: Think it through with Hooty.

activities.title: Fastest Transport
activities.prompt: Which statement matches air travel?
options: It is the fastest form of transport.
It starts the regional aviation market.
It supports oil and natural gas operations.
It is called the Regional Connectivity Scheme.
activities.explanation: Your lesson describes air travel as the fastest and most comfortable transport.

activities.title: UDAN
activities.prompt: The Regional Connectivity Scheme is called ______.
activities.hint: This short name begins with U.
activities.explanation: UDAN is the short name for the Regional Connectivity Scheme.

activities.title: The Purpose of UDAN
activities.prompt: The UDAN scheme was designed to stop the regional aviation market.
activities.explanation: UDAN was designed to start the regional aviation market. It also encourages airlines to serve regional routes.

activities.title: The Aim of UDAN
activities.prompt: What does UDAN aim to achieve?
options: Make flying affordable for ordinary citizens.
Make flying costly for ordinary citizens.
Encourage airlines to avoid regional routes.
Discourage useful policies and incentives.
activities.explanation: UDAN aims to make flying affordable for ordinary citizens. Useful policies encourage airlines to serve regional routes.

activities.title: Match Each Name
activities.prompt: Match each name with its correct description.
pairs: Designed to start the regional aviation market
Support oil and natural gas operations
activities.explanation: Each left-hand item is paired with its description from the lesson.

activities.title: Helicopter Reach
activities.prompt: Helicopters cannot reach difficult terrain in the north-east.
activities.explanation: Helicopters can reach difficult terrain in the north-east and the listed northern states.

activities.title: Helicopter Support
activities.prompt: Put these steps in order to describe helicopter support.
items: Helicopter services support operations in inaccessible areas.
Oil and natural gas operations receive this support.
activities.explanation: Helicopters first reach difficult terrain. Their services support oil and natural gas operations in inaccessible areas.

activities.prompt: A map shows northern rivers and forests. What does it suggest?
options: Air travel may help where land travel is hard.
Air travel will be best in every kind of place.
Land travel will always be easy in that region.
Every remote town will soon have an airport.

why.Air travel will be best in every kind of: This mistake treats fastest air travel as best everywhere.
why.Land travel will always be easy in that: This mistake ignores what the map shows about difficult land travel.
why.Every remote town will soon have an airp: This mistake assumes the map predicts new airports in every town.

activities.explanation: This is right because rivers and forests make land travel difficult there.

activities.prompt: Useful incentives help airlines open remote routes. What is the likely result?
options: More airlines stop serving regional places.
More regional and remote routes are served.
Only crowded city routes get new flights.
Remote routes become costlier for airlines.

why.More airlines stop serving regional plac: This mistake thinks incentives make airlines leave regional places.
why.Only crowded city routes get new flights: This mistake focuses only on large cities instead of remote routes.
why.Remote routes become costlier for airlin: This mistake assumes support makes remote routes costlier.

activities.explanation: This is right because incentives encourage airlines to serve these routes.
